Translation
trans-LAY-shun
n. (a being carried or removed from one place or state to another, here from earth to heaven without death)
Latin translatio, from trans-, across, and ferre, to carry — a carrying across from one state of existence to another.

Biblical Definition

By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death; and was not found, because God had translated him: for before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God.

Enoch's translation is the Old Testament's own anticipation of a hope the New Testament will later generalize to every believer: removal from this life into God's presence without passing through death at all. The writer to the Hebrews is careful about the order of events — for before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God — making plain that the translation was the reward of a settled walk with God (Gen 5:24, walked with God, and he was not), not an isolated miracle detached from the character it crowned. Translation here stands as a down payment on the resurrection hope: proof within the Old Testament itself that God has power to remove his people from death's reach entirely, whenever and however he chooses.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from TRANSLATIO (L.): removal from one place or state to another; here, removal from earthly life to heaven without death.

expand to see more

TRANSLATE, v.t. To remove from one place or condition to another.

TRANSLATION, n. The act of translating; a removal or transfer.

In Hebrews, specifically removal from earthly life without death.

Explicitly tied to Enoch's prior testimony of pleasing God.

Functions as an Old Testament anticipation of resurrection hope.

Key Scripture

Heb 11:5 — "By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death; and was not found, because God had translated him: for before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God."

Modern Corruption

Fascination with Enoch's translation can drift toward speculative curiosity about where he went or what he saw, while Hebrews keeps the emphasis squarely on the faith and the settled, pleasing walk with God that preceded and explained it.

expand to see more

Popular curiosity about Enoch tends to chase extra-biblical speculation about his translation's destination or circumstances. Hebrews 11 is notably restrained, offering no such detail and instead doubling back to the testimony that preceded the event.

The corrective is to let the text's own emphasis stand: by faith Enoch was translated, and the faith is defined by a settled, long walk of pleasing God, not by the spectacular nature of his removal. The event crowns a character; it is not presented as interesting apart from it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew laqach, to take, from Genesis 5:24 (God took him), rendered in the Septuagint and here in Hebrews with the Greek metetethe, to transfer or change place — the same root used of changing the priesthood in Hebrews 7:12.
